stem.text: White-clawed crayfish, Austropotamobius pallipes, live in rivers and lakes in Europe.

In the 1850s, the North American signal crayfish, Pacifastacus leniusculus, was introduced to Europe. The introduced species carried a pathogen that causes a disease known as crayfish plague. This disease kills A. pallipes.
Since 1850, the population size of A. pallipes has reduced in many areas of Europe due to the spread of crayfish plague.
North American P. leniusculus can carry the crayfish plague pathogen without showing symptoms because they have evolved resistance to it.
Explain how P. leniusculus could have evolved resistance to the crayfish plague pathogen.

points.text: pathogen / disease / plague, was selection pressure ;
mutation, gave selective advantage / was selected for / allowed crayfish to survive (plague) ;
survivors / resistant crayfish, bred / reproduced / passed on mutation ;
frequency of, allele / mutation, (for resistance) increased ;

explanation.text: A random mutation arising in some individuals happened to give resistance to the pathogen. Once the pathogen was present, it acted as a selection pressure: non-resistant crayfish died, but resistant individuals survived and reproduced, passing the resistance allele to their offspring. Over generations the allele frequency for resistance increased in the population, an example of natural (directional) selection.

reasoningChain: A mutation arose that happened to confer resistance to the crayfish plague pathogen.
The pathogen acts as a selection pressure once it is present.
Resistant individuals survive and reproduce, passing the allele to offspring.
The allele for resistance increases in frequency over generations: natural selection.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing the mutation as arising in response to the pathogen, rather than as a pre-existing random change that the pathogen then selected for.

stem.text: It is difficult to locate crayfish because they live underwater.
After an outbreak of crayfish plague in one country in Europe, researchers used an environmental DNA technique to find the locations in a river where populations of A. pallipes were still surviving.

Water samples were taken from locations along the river. Each water sample was filtered to obtain any cells or DNA that had been released by organisms into the water. The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was carried out on this DNA using primers specific to A. pallipes DNA.
Outline and explain the steps that occur in PCR.

points.text: (heat to) 90–98 °C so DNA, denatures / strands separate ;
(cool to) 50–65 °C so primers, bind / base pair / anneal (to DNA) ;
(heat to) 68–75 °C so, Taq / DNA, polymerase, makes DNA / (new) strand ;

explanation.text: PCR cycles through three temperatures. Heating to 90-98°C breaks the hydrogen bonds holding the two DNA strands together, so they separate (denature). Cooling to 50-65°C lets short primers, specific to the target sequence, bind to the single strands by complementary base pairing. Heating to 68-75°C is the optimum temperature for Taq polymerase (a heat-stable DNA polymerase) to extend the primers and build new complementary strands. Repeating this cycle doubles the amount of target DNA each time, amplifying it exponentially.

reasoningChain: Heat to around 90-98°C to denature the double-stranded DNA into single strands.
Cool to around 50-65°C so primers anneal to the single strands at the target sequence.
Heat to around 68-75°C so Taq polymerase extends the primers into new strands.
Repeat the cycle many times to amplify the DNA exponentially.

inferredMistakes.text: Naming the three steps (denaturation, annealing, extension) without giving the approximate temperature for each, when the question asks to explain the steps.

stem.text: Suggest how the researchers were able to discover suitable sequences for the primers.

explanation.text: To design primers specific to A. pallipes DNA, the researchers would need to know its DNA sequence (or a sequence unique to it compared with other species). This kind of sequence information is held in biological databases, which can be searched using bioinformatics tools to find or confirm a species-specific sequence to target.

reasoningChain: Primers must match a sequence unique to A. pallipes.
That sequence information comes from a genome/DNA sequence database, searched with bioinformatics tools.

stem.text: The PCR technique used in this research is quantitative. A fluorescent dye binds to the DNA and the fluorescence is monitored throughout the process, showing the quantity of DNA present.
Fig. 4.1 shows standard curves for four known concentrations of DNA, A, B, C and D, and the result obtained for A. pallipes DNA at one location along the river (dotted line).

stem.caption: Fig. 4.1
stem.alt: Graph of fluorescence (log scale) against PCR cycle number, with four S-shaped curves labelled A, B, C and D (reaching the fluorescence threshold at successively higher cycle numbers: A around cycle 12, B around 16, C around 20, D around 27) and a dotted curve for the sample, reaching the threshold at 28 cycles, between curves C and D.

stem.text: State the letter of the curve with the highest starting concentration of DNA.

markScheme.note: 此小问的 MS 原文在第 9 页（4(c) 部分），文本提取定位在页 9 开头，文件内 source.ms 已标 9。

explanation.text: The sample with more starting DNA reaches the fluorescence threshold in fewer cycles, because there is already more template to amplify. Curve A crosses the threshold first (at the lowest cycle number), so it had the highest starting concentration.

reasoningChain: More starting DNA means fewer cycles are needed to reach the fluorescence threshold.
Curve A reaches the threshold at the lowest cycle number, so it has the highest starting concentration.

inferredMistakes.text: Picking the curve that reaches the highest final fluorescence, rather than the one reaching the threshold first.

stem.text: The quantity of A. pallipes DNA reaches a threshold (marked as a horizontal line on Fig. 4.1) at 28 cycles. The DNA in curve C reaches the threshold after 25 cycles. In one cycle of PCR the concentration of DNA doubles.
Calculate the relative difference in the starting concentrations of A. pallipes DNA and the DNA in curve C.

explanation.text: Curve C reaches the threshold 3 cycles before the sample (28 - 25 = 3). Since concentration doubles every cycle, starting 3 cycles ahead means curve C started with 2^3 = 8 times more DNA than the A. pallipes sample.

reasoningChain: Find the difference in cycle number: 28 - 25 = 3 cycles.
Each cycle doubles the DNA, so the difference in starting concentration is 2^3 = 8 times.

inferredMistakes.text: Multiplying the cycle difference by 2 instead of raising 2 to the power of the cycle difference.

stem.text: Fluorescent molecules have other uses in gene technology.
Fig. 4.2 shows an agar plate with normal bacteria and genetically modified bacteria. The genetically modified bacteria make a green fluorescent protein.

stem.caption: Fig. 4.2
stem.alt: Diagram of a circular agar plate viewed from above, with a streak of normal bacteria on the left half and a streak of genetically modified fluorescent bacteria on the right half.

stem.text: Identify the component that is taken up by normal bacteria to produce the genetically modified bacteria in Fig. 4.2 and state what this component contains to allow the bacteria to make green fluorescent protein.

explanation.text: Bacteria take up genetic material in the form of a plasmid, a circular piece of DNA that can be taken up and replicated independently of the bacterial chromosome. For the bacteria to actually produce green fluorescent protein, the plasmid must contain the gene for that protein, and a promoter so the bacterium's own transcription machinery can recognise where to start transcribing that gene.

reasoningChain: Identify the vector bacteria take up: a plasmid.
State what must be on it for the protein to be made: the gene for green fluorescent protein.
State what else is needed for that gene to be transcribed: a promoter.

inferredMistakes.text: Naming only the plasmid without going on to say what it must contain (the gene and a promoter) to actually produce the protein.

stem.text: Suggest why the gene for green fluorescent protein is sometimes transferred in addition to the desired gene in genetic engineering.

points.text: to act as a, marker / reporter, gene ;
alternatives: to identify, recombinant / GM / transgenic, bacteria / organisms
to show expression of another transferred gene

explanation.text: Green fluorescent protein glows and is easy to detect. If it is transferred alongside the gene of interest, bacteria that fluoresce can be identified as ones that successfully took up and are expressing the transferred DNA, acting as a visible marker for successful genetic engineering.

reasoningChain: GFP is easy to detect because it fluoresces.
If linked to the gene of interest, its presence confirms the desired gene has also been taken up and expressed.
